paperTitle: Singapore-Cambridge GCE O-Level 1184 English Language — AI-authored Practice Paper 38: The Red Packet (Paper 2 §B style)

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [15 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
On the first morning of Chinese New Year our flat filled with relatives, and I went from one to the next with both hands out and a practised greeting. I was fifteen that year, old enough to know better and young enough not to. In my head I kept a running total of the red packets stuffed into my pocket, and I could hardly wait for the last guest to leave so that I could shut my door and count them properly.

Paragraph 2
Gu Po came late, as she always did, having taken two buses from her one-room rental flat. She was my grandmother's younger sister, frail now, her back curved like a question mark, and she held the doorframe for a moment before stepping in. My mother hurried to take her bag. Gu Po waved her away, straightened her blouse, and began greeting each of us in turn as though she were the one with something to give.

Paragraph 3
When my turn came she pressed a red packet into my palm with both of her hands, the way one passes something important. Later, alone in my room, I tore through the pile. Hers held a single two-dollar note, crumpled and soft, and it lay in my palm like a dried leaf. I barely looked at it. I set it on the desk with the loose coins and went back to the thicker packets, and by evening I had forgotten which one had been hers.

Paragraph 4
A fortnight later my mother asked me to carry a tin of biscuits to Gu Po's flat. I had not been there in years. One room held everything she owned: a folding table, a thin mattress rolled against the wall, a calendar from a provision shop that had closed long ago. The place was sparse in a way I had no word for then. She insisted on opening the tin I had brought and feeding me four of the biscuits, one after another, refusing to take any herself.

Paragraph 5
On the bus home my mother told me, in the flat voice she uses for things she has decided I am finally old enough to hear, that Gu Po lives on a small government allowance and what she earns collecting cardboard from the back lanes. From the middle of the year she begins putting coins into an old milk tin, one or two at a time, so that when the New Year comes there is a packet for every child in the family. She has never once let a year pass without giving.

Paragraph 6
I looked out of the window for a long while and did not trust myself to speak. My face was burning, and I was glad my mother had turned away. I thought about the thick packets I had counted so greedily, handed over without a thought by uncles who would not miss the money, and about two dollars carried on two buses by a woman who had gone without to save it. I had weighed her gift on the wrong scale entirely. The smallest packet in the pile had cost more than all the others put together.

Paragraph 7
That night I went through my drawer until I found it, the two-dollar note with its soft creases, and I did not spend it. I still have it. Years of folding have worn it until it feels more like cloth than paper, and every time my wallet falls open on it I see a woman with a curved back straightening her blouse in a doorway, insisting on being the one who gives.

(Glossary: Gu Po: a Chinese term of address for a grand-aunt, one's grandmother's sister. red packet / hongbao: a red envelope containing money, given to children and unmarried younger relatives at Chinese New Year. one-room rental flat: the smallest and most heavily subsidised public housing in Singapore.)

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 2, how did Gu Po travel to the family's flat? [1]
questions.answer: she took two buses (from her one-room rental flat)

questions.stem: Q2. From Paragraph 3, how much money was inside Gu Po's red packet? [1]
Q3. What does the word 'frail' in 'frail now, her back curved like a question mark' (Paragraph 2) suggest about Gu Po? [1]
questions.answer: that she was weak and delicate, her body worn by old age

questions.stem: Q4. What does the word 'crumpled' in 'a single two-dollar note, crumpled and soft' (Paragraph 3) suggest about the note? [1]
questions.answer: that it was creased and wrinkled / crushed rather than crisp and new

questions.stem: Q5. What does the word 'sparse' in 'The place was sparse' (Paragraph 4) suggest about Gu Po's flat? [1]
questions.answer: that it was bare, containing very few possessions

questions.stem: Q6. Using your own words, explain what Gu Po's behaviour during the narrator's visit shows about the kind of person she is. (Paragraph 4) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (hospitality): although she owns almost nothing, she immediately opened the tin of biscuits that had been brought for her and served them to her visitor — her instinct is to feed the person who came to see her; MP2 (she puts others before herself): she fed him four biscuits one after another while refusing to eat a single one, going without so that her guest could have them. Award one mark per distinct point. NOTE for markers: 'she wanted to be the giver, not the one pitied' belongs to Q7 — do NOT award it here as well.

questions.stem: Q7. Using your own words, explain why Gu Po gave a red packet to every child even though she had so little. (Paragraphs 2 and 5) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (dignity / not being pitied): giving at New Year let her arrive as the one with something to offer rather than as a poor relative to be helped. ALSO ACCEPT for MP1: it was a tradition/rule she refused to break ('She has never once let a year pass without giving'). MP2 (love expressed through sacrifice): saving coins from the middle of the year was how she showed she cared for every child in the family, even though it meant going without herself. Award one mark per distinct point. Gu Po's motive is never stated outright, so credit any well-reasoned answer anchored in Paragraph 2 or 5.

questions.stem: Q8. Using your own words, explain what the narrator means by saying he 'had weighed her gift on the wrong scale entirely'. (Paragraph 6) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (the wrong measure): he had judged the packet only by the amount of money inside it; MP2 (the right measure): a gift should be judged by what it costs the giver, and by that measure hers — months of saved coins from someone who had almost nothing — was worth more than all the rich uncles' packets. Award one mark per distinct point.

questions.stem: Q9. What is the effect of describing the two-dollar note lying in the narrator's palm 'like a dried leaf' (Paragraph 3)? [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (the image itself): a dried leaf is small, thin, dry and faded — the shrivelled remains of something that was once alive; MP2 (the effect): this conveys exactly how worthless the note seemed to the narrator at that moment, and how casually he brushed it aside. Award one mark per distinct point. Credit as an ALTERNATIVE to MP2: the dried leaf also quietly echoes Gu Po's own frailty and age.

questions.stem: Q10. What is the effect of the closing detail that years of folding have worn the note 'until it feels more like cloth than paper' (Paragraph 7)? [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (what the wear records): paper only turns soft as cloth after years of being folded and carried, so the note's worn state is physical proof of how long the narrator has kept it on him; MP2 (the reversal): the same two dollars he once dropped among the loose coins have become a treasured keepsake, valued now for what they mean rather than what they are worth. Award one mark per distinct point. Accept 'he has carried it with him for years' — the wear comes from carrying it, not necessarily from taking it out to look at.

sections.instruction: Q11. [4 marks in total] The narrator's dominant feeling changes as the passage moves from the New Year morning to the years that follow. For each moment below, go back to the relevant paragraphs of the narrative and choose ONE word from the bank that best describes his dominant feeling there. Some words in the bank are not used, and each word may be used once only. Word bank: amused / ashamed / bored / dismissive / eager / humbled / jealous / puzzled.
sections.passage: Refer to the same 'The Red Packet' narrative in Exercise 1 above. Read the paragraphs named in each question, then choose the single word from the bank that best describes how the narrator feels at that moment.
